name: Figs
summary: One of the first fruits people grew, rich in fibre, especially when dried. In small trials figs eased constipation; there's little other research on eating them.
inIt: A fig is not a single fruit in the usual sense. It is a closed, hollow flower head with hundreds of tiny flowers inside; what people eat is the fleshy wall and the many small fruits (the 'seeds') that form from those flowers.

The UK food table (CoFID) measures the basic nutrients. Per 100 g, fresh figs ('Figs, whole green fruit, raw') have 43 kcal, 9.5 g of sugars, 200 mg of potassium and 38 mg of calcium. Dried figs ('Figs, whole fruit, dried') have 227 kcal, 52.9 g of sugars, 970 mg of potassium, 250 mg of calcium, 80 mg of magnesium and 4.2 mg of iron. The table has no fibre value for either of these two foods, and no vitamin K value for any fig.

Fibre measured elsewhere: in figs from eastern Morocco, fresh figs had about 2.2 to 2.6 g of fibre per 100 g and sun-dried figs 5.6 to 6.2 g. The UK table lists 10 g of fibre per 100 g for ready-to-eat semi-dried figs (CoFID 14-395).

Figs contain polyphenols, among them phenolic acids, flavonoids such as rutin, catechin and epicatechin, and anthocyanins (the purple colour). The main anthocyanin is cyanidin-3-rutinoside. In a study of six varieties, darker figs (black Mission, red Brown Turkey) had more polyphenols, flavonoids and anthocyanins than lighter green or yellow figs, and most of them were in the skin rather than the pulp. The food table measures none of these.

The milky sap (latex) of the tree, leaves and fruit skin holds ficin, an enzyme that breaks down proteins. Cheesemakers use it to curdle milk; Homer's Iliad mentions fig juice curdling milk, and Hippocrates and Aristotle wrote about fig latex used this way.

Fig leaves, twigs and roots contain furanocoumarins such as psoralen and bergapten, compounds that make skin burn in sunlight. A 2026 study comparing fruits, leaves and twigs found furanocoumarins among the main compounds in leaves and twigs, with the most in leaves; a 2013 review also lists psoralen and bergapten found in fruit pulp and peel. A genome study found roots held the most psoralen.
In 10 people, eating 40 g of dried figs raised the antioxidant capacity of the blood for about 4 hours. That is a laboratory measure, not a health outcome.
Nobody knows which compounds, if any, explain effects seen in trials. Fibre is the usual explanation for constipation results, but a food has thousands of compounds that food tables don't track.

lore.who: Ancient Greece (Diogenes Laertius, about 200 AD)
lore.belief: Diogenes Laertius reports that athletes in earlier times trained on dried figs, soft cheese and wheatmeal, until a diet of meat replaced it (credited to Pythagoras, who first tried it on the athlete Eurymenes).
lore.note: Told as a report of older practice, not an observation of his own day; he says others credit a different Pythagoras, a trainer. Hicks's translation prints 'butter' with a footnote 'or rather soft cheese'.

sources.title: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book 8 (Pythagoras), section 12, translated by R. D. Hicks
sources.author: Diogenes Laertius

sources.title: From Olympia to Atlanta: a cultural-historical perspective on diet and athletic training (abstract: Diogenes Laertius wrote that Greek athletes trained on dried figs, moist cheese and wheat; then the pattern changed and focused on meat)
sources.author: Grivetti LE, Applegate EA

lore.who: Ancient Rome (Pliny the Elder, about 77 AD)
lore.belief: Pliny says dried figs are nourishing and invigorating, which is why athletes in former times used them as their food, until the gymnast Pythagoras first brought in a flesh diet.
lore.note: Same tradition as Diogenes Laertius, set down earlier; Pliny gives the reason he thought they were chosen.

sources.title: Pliny the Elder, Natural History, Book 23, chapter 63 (Figs: one hundred and eleven observations upon them), translated by Bostock and Riley
sources.author: Pliny the Elder

lore.who: Ancient Greece (Plato, about 375 BC)
lore.belief: In the Republic Socrates describes a plain city whose people have figs, chickpeas and beans as dessert, along with olives, cheese and boiled greens, and expects them to live in peace and health and die in old age.
lore.note: Figs are one of several simple foods in an imagined city, not singled out for a health effect; Glaucon mocks it as a 'city of pigs'.

sources.title: Plato, Republic, Book 2, 372c-d, translated by Paul Shorey
sources.author: Plato

lore.who: Ancient Greece (Hippocratic Regimen, about 400 BC)
lore.belief: The Regimen says the green fig moistens, warms and passes well by stool, that the latest crop of figs is the best and the first the worst, and that dry figs are 'burning' but also pass well by stool.
lore.note: Told in the writer's terms of hot, cold, moist and dry.

sources.title: Hippocrates, Regimen II, chapter 55 (fruits), Loeb Classical Library vol. IV, translated by W. H. S. Jones (scan, p. 336)
sources.author: Hippocratic Corpus

lore.who: Ancient Greece (Hippocratic Regimen, about 400 BC)
lore.belief: The Regimen says millet groats and husks eaten with figs make strong nourishment for hard workers.
lore.note: A passing remark in a list of grains and pulses, not a claim about figs alone.

sources.title: Hippocrates, Regimen II, chapter 45 (grains and pulses), Loeb Classical Library vol. IV, translated by W. H. S. Jones
sources.author: Hippocratic Corpus

lore.who: Ancient Greece (Herodotus of Lycia, quoted by Athenaeus, about 200 AD)
lore.belief: The physician Herodotus of Lycia, in a treatise on figs, argued that figs are more useful to people than any other tree fruit and that new-born children grow sturdy when fed fig juice.
lore.note: Herodotus of Lycia's own treatise is lost; this is Athenaeus's report of it, spoken by a character at a dinner.

sources.title: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae, Book 3, section 78d-e (Loeb, translated by C. B. Gulick)
sources.author: Athenaeus

lore.who: Ancient Greece (the comic poet Pherecrates, quoted by Athenaeus)
lore.belief: In Pherecrates's play The Persians a character says that anyone who finds a fresh fig smears it on babies' eyes, which Athenaeus takes as a sign that people thought figs an uncommonly good remedy.
lore.note: A line from a comedy, so a sign of a folk belief, not a medical text.

sources.title: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae, Book 3, section 78e (Loeb, translated by C. B. Gulick)
sources.author: Athenaeus

lore.who: Ancient Greece (the physician Phylotimus, quoted by Athenaeus)
lore.belief: Phylotimus held that ripe fresh figs are digested more easily than other fruit, do not hinder the digestion of other food eaten with them, and cause a copious, quick and painless loosening of the bowels.
lore.note: Phylotimus's book On Food survives only in quotation. He also noted that figs left the hands both sticky and clean.

sources.title: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae, Book 3, section 79b-d (Loeb, translated by C. B. Gulick)
sources.author: Athenaeus

lore.who: Ancient Greece (comic poets and the physician Diphilus of Siphnos, quoted by Athenaeus)
lore.belief: Greek comic poets joked that figs eaten at midday bring on fever and vomiting of bile, and the physician Diphilus of Siphnos said fresh figs are only slightly nourishing and make poor chyle but pass easily and are better when ripened naturally in season.
lore.note: Two separate beliefs quoted together by Athenaeus; the midday-fig lines come from plays by Pherecrates, Aristophanes, Eubulus and Nicophon.

sources.title: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae, Book 3, section 80a-c (Loeb, translated by C. B. Gulick)
sources.author: Athenaeus

lore.who: Ancient Greece and Rome (Demetrius of Scepsis, quoted by Athenaeus; Pliny the Elder)
lore.belief: Demetrius of Scepsis said people who abstain from figs have good voices, citing the actor Hegesianax, who found his pleasing voice after eighteen years without them, and Pliny likewise says it is generally thought that figs spoil the voice.
lore.note: Both treat it as a common belief; Demetrius's anecdote is the only evidence offered.

sources.title: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae, Book 3, section 80d (Loeb, translated by C. B. Gulick)
sources.author: Athenaeus

sources.author: Pliny the Elder

lore.who: Ancient Rome (Pliny the Elder, about 77 AD)
lore.belief: Pliny says ripe figs are diuretic and laxative, that dried figs are wonderfully good for the throat and fauces, and that figs boiled with hyssop cure inveterate coughs.
lore.note: He also says dried figs are bad for the stomach and cause thirst; these are separate points in the same chapter.

sources.title: Pliny the Elder, Natural History, Book 23, chapter 63 (Figs: one hundred and eleven observations upon them), translated by Bostock and Riley
sources.author: Pliny the Elder

lore.who: Ancient Rome (Pliny the Elder, about 77 AD)
lore.belief: Pliny says ripe figs allay thirst and are cooling, so they should not be refused in the fevers he calls 'stegnae', and that fig ash rubbed on with oil cures weakness of sight.
lore.note: The ash belief is about the burnt wood, not the fruit.

sources.title: Pliny the Elder, Natural History, Book 23, chapter 63
sources.author: Pliny the Elder

lore.who: Ancient Rome (Celsus, about 30 AD)
lore.belief: Celsus recommends a gargle made from dried figs (with hyssop, thyme and other herbs) for a sore throat, and for a chronic cough a few very juicy figs cooked over charcoal after exercises.
lore.note: Figs are one item among several in each remedy; he also uses a fig-and-honey-wine gargle for throat swellings.

sources.title: Celsus, De Medicina, Book 4, chapter 7, section 3 (gargle with dried figs) and chapter 10, section 1 (figs for chronic cough), Loeb translation by W. G. Spencer
sources.author: Celsus

sources.title: Celsus, De Medicina, Book 6, chapter 10, section 3 (gargle of fig and honey wine)
sources.author: Celsus

lore.who: Ancient Rome (Celsus, about 30 AD)
lore.belief: For a patient with pain in the side, Celsus gives a drink of hyssop boiled with a dried fig, and for a gut illness in which the bowels void nothing he lists green figs in season, taken a little at a time, among the ways to loosen them.
lore.note: Both are minor parts of longer treatments.

sources.title: Celsus, De Medicina, Book 4, chapter 14, section 2 (hyssop and dried fig drink) and chapter 19, section 2 (green figs to loosen the bowels), Loeb translation by W. G. Spencer
sources.author: Celsus

lore.who: Ancient Rome (Pliny the Elder, Natural History, about AD 77)
lore.belief: Pliny wrote that dried figs, though hard on the stomach, were good in every case for the bladder, for laboured breathing and asthma, and for diseases of the liver, kidneys and spleen.
lore.note: No study on this page has tested figs for asthma or breathing, or for the bladder, liver, kidneys or spleen.

sources.title: Pliny the Elder, Natural History, book 23, chapter 63 (translated by J. Bostock and H. T. Riley)
sources.author: Pliny the Elder

lore.who: Ancient Rome (Pliny the Elder, Natural History, about AD 77)
lore.belief: Pliny wrote that figs were extremely useful for people recovering from a long illness, and for people with epilepsy or dropsy (swelling from fluid held in the body).
lore.note: No study has tested figs in people recovering from an illness, or in epilepsy or fluid swelling.

sources.title: Pliny the Elder, Natural History, book 23, chapter 63 (translated by J. Bostock and H. T. Riley)
sources.author: Pliny the Elder

lore.who: Ancient Rome (Pliny the Elder, Natural History, about AD 77)
lore.belief: Pliny warned that ripe figs make people sweat and bring out pimples, which made them unwholesome in autumn, when the sweating was followed by shivering; that they upset the stomach for a short time; that they were generally thought to spoil the voice; and that figs forced to ripen early were never wholesome.
lore.note: None of these warnings has been studied: no study on this page looked at sweating, pimples, shivering or the voice after eating figs.

sources.title: Pliny the Elder, Natural History, book 23, chapter 63 (translated by J. Bostock and H. T. Riley)
sources.author: Pliny the Elder

lore.who: Babylonian Talmud (Yoma 83b, compiled about the 6th century AD)
lore.belief: The rabbis taught that a person seized by bulmos, a sudden, faint, ravenous hunger, was to be fed honey and sweet foods. Rabbi Yohanan told how, seized by it once, he ran to the east side of a fig tree, where the sun ripens the figs first, found ripe figs, ate them and was saved.
lore.note: Bulmos isn't a term modern medicine uses. No study on this page has tested figs for sudden weakness from hunger.

sources.title: Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 83b (William Davidson translation)
sources.author: Talmud

lore.who: Chinese medicine (Wang Ying and Li Shizhen, in the Bencao Gangmu, 1578)
lore.belief: Chinese physicians wrote that the fig fruit opens the appetite and stops diarrhoea (Wang Ying), and Li Shizhen added that it treats the 'five kinds of piles'; for painful, swollen piles a hot brew of the leaves was used to steam and wash them.
lore.note: No study on this page has tested figs for appetite, diarrhoea or piles. The small trials found something close to the opposite of stopping diarrhoea: figs loosened stools in people with constipation.

sources.title: Bencao Gangmu (Compendium of Materia Medica), fruits 3: fig (Chinese text)
sources.author: Li Shizhen

lore.who: Hebrew Bible and the Talmud
lore.belief: In Genesis, once Adam and Eve had eaten from the forbidden tree, they saw they were naked and sewed fig leaves together to cover themselves. The rabbis of the Talmud argued over which tree it had been: Rabbi Nehemiah said a fig, because they mended their shame with the same tree that had caused it; Rabbi Meir said a vine and Rabbi Judah wheat.
lore.note: Genesis never names the fruit. The apple of later European art isn't in the text.

sources.title: Genesis 3:7 (JPS Tanakh)
sources.author: Hebrew Bible

sources.author: Talmud

lore.who: Hebrew Bible (2 Kings and Micah)
lore.belief: When King Hezekiah lay dangerously ill and was told he would die, he prayed, and God promised to heal him; the prophet Isaiah then had a cake of figs laid on his rash (a boil in older translations), and he recovered. For the prophets the fig tree also meant peace: in days to come, Micah said, every family would sit under its own vine and fig tree with no one to disturb them.
lore.note: In the story the healing comes from God, with the figs as the means. No trial found for this page has tested figs laid on the skin; the fig trials are of eating them.

sources.title: 2 Kings 20:1-7 (JPS Tanakh)
sources.author: Hebrew Bible

sources.title: Micah 4:4 (JPS Tanakh)
sources.author: Hebrew Bible

lore.who: Ancient Rome (Livy and Pliny the Elder)
lore.belief: Romans believed the twins Romulus and Remus, founders of Rome, were left by the flooded Tiber beneath a fig tree, where a she-wolf found and suckled them. A fig tree kept in memory of it, the Ficus Ruminalis, grew in the Forum; when it withered, people took it as an evil omen, and the priests replaced it.

sources.title: Livy, History of Rome, book 1, chapter 4 (translated by Canon Roberts)
sources.author: Livy

sources.title: Pliny the Elder, Natural History, book 15, chapter 20 (translated by J. Bostock and H. T. Riley)
sources.author: Pliny the Elder

lore.who: Ancient Rome (Cato the Elder, 2nd century BC, as told by Pliny)
lore.belief: Cato, who cried at every sitting of the Senate that Carthage must be destroyed, once held up a ripe fig and asked the senators when they thought it had been picked. When they agreed it was fresh, he told them it had been picked at Carthage two days before: so close was the enemy. The third war with Carthage, in which the city was destroyed, began soon after.

sources.title: Pliny the Elder, Natural History, book 15, chapter 20 (translated by J. Bostock and H. T. Riley)
sources.author: Pliny the Elder

lore.who: Ancient Rome (Pliny the Elder, Natural History, 1st century AD)
lore.belief: Pliny wrote that figs invigorate the young, improve the health of the old and slow the forming of wrinkles, that they are nourishing and strengthening, and that athletes in earlier times lived on them.
lore.note: No study has tested figs for strength, ageing or wrinkles.

sources.author: Pliny the Elder

lore.who: Christianity (the Gospel of Mark)
lore.belief: Mark tells that Jesus, hungry on the way into Jerusalem, came to a fig tree in leaf but found no fruit on it, for it wasn't the season for figs, and said that no one would ever eat from it again. The next morning his disciples saw it withered from the roots, and he used it to teach them about faith.

sources.title: Gospel of Mark, chapter 11, verses 12-14 and 20-24 (King James Version)
sources.author: New Testament

history.who: Early Neolithic Jordan Valley (Gilgal I, about 11,400 to 11,200 years ago)
history.use: Figs gathered and stored as food. Archaeologists found nine charred figs from trees that fruit without pollination and suggested people grew them from planted branches, which would make the fig one of the first cultivated plants.
history.note: This is about food, not medicine. Other scientists replied that such trees also produce seeded figs and can spread on their own, so the find doesn't prove cultivation, and a 2026 genetic study of 949 fig trees suggests figs were domesticated in several Mediterranean regions rather than in one place.

sources.title: Early domesticated fig in the Jordan Valley.
Comment on "Early domesticated fig in the Jordan Valley".
Diffuse and regionally structured domestication of the common fig (Ficus carica L.) in the Mediterranean Basin.

history.who: Ancient Greece and Rome (Dioscorides, De Materia Medica, 1st century CE)
history.use: Fig as a general tonic. In a study of medical books from antiquity to today, fig and wormwood were the only ones of 102 plants recorded as general tonics in the ancient source, Dioscorides.
history.note: A 'general tonic' isn't something trials measure. No study has tested whether eating figs makes people generally stronger or healthier.

sources.title: Trends of Medicinal Plant Use over the Last 2000 Years in Central Europe.

history.who: Dioscorides (1st century CE) and folk medicine in Albania, Cyprus, Greece and Turkey
history.use: Fig for skin complaints. A 2022 review found fig among the most cited plants for skin problems in modern folk medicine of the region (72 recorded uses), and listed it among plants Dioscorides also described for some of the same skin complaints.
history.note: No trial has tested fig fruit on the skin. The sap and leaves can do the opposite of healing: they can burn skin that is then exposed to sunlight (see who should be careful).

sources.title: Medicinal Plants Used Traditionally for Skin Related Problems in the South Balkan and East Mediterranean Region-A Review.

history.use: Fig fruit and leaf among the ingredients of remedies for diabetes; one remedy was eaten with dried figs and raisins.
history.note: Apart from one small trial that couldn't be checked, eating figs alone hasn't been tested in diabetes. In a trial of mixed dried fruit (a quarter of it figs), fasting blood sugar was very slightly higher than with a starchy snack. Studies of fig leaves and fig extracts are different products.

sources.title: Diabetes and traditional remedies in Medieval Persia: a historical perspective.

processing: Drying takes out most of the water, so sugars, fibre and minerals are packed into less weight. In the UK food table, 100 g of dried figs have 52.9 g of sugars against 9.5 g in 100 g of fresh figs, and 970 mg of potassium against 200 mg. In Moroccan figs, sun-drying raised sugars from about 15 g to 52 to 54 g per 100 g and fibre from about 2.3 to 2.5 g to 5.6 to 6.2 g.

Studies disagree on what drying does to polyphenols. One study found more total phenolics after sun- or oven-drying (but less of the main anthocyanin); another found that drying lowered phenols when compared on a dry-weight basis; in Moroccan figs, sun-drying raised phenolic content but lowered flavonoids and vitamin C.
Dark-skinned figs have more polyphenols and anthocyanins than green or yellow ones, and the skin holds most of them, so peeled figs have less.

Fig leaf tea and fig leaf extracts are different products from the fruit, with different compounds (more furanocoumarins, for example). Trials of fig leaf tea, such as one in mild eczema, and of fig fruit extracts in drinks, are not evidence for eating figs.
The UK food table's fresh fig is labelled 'Figs, whole green fruit, raw'. The table also has semi-dried ready-to-eat figs (14-395) and dried figs stewed with or without sugar.
whatStudiesDid: Very few trials gave people figs to eat. A Korean trial gave 80 people with functional constipation a fig paste or a placebo every day for 8 weeks (300 g a day, according to a 2022 meta-analysis's table). An Iranian trial gave people with irritable bowel syndrome with constipation dried figs, 45 g twice a day (90 g a day), for 4 months. A US trial had 83 adults with raised LDL cholesterol add 120 g of dried California Mission figs a day to their usual diet for 5 weeks, then eat their usual diet for 5 weeks, or the other way round. Another US trial gave 55 adults three-quarters of a cup a day of mixed dried plums, figs, dates and raisins, or a starchy snack, for 4 weeks each. Trials of fig syrups (cooked preparations, some with walnut) were also done in pregnant women and children with constipation.

findings.population: Korean adults with functional constipation (one trial of a fig paste); pregnant women and children in small Iranian trials of fig syrup
whyThisGrade: Only one placebo-controlled trial of a fig product eaten as food: 80 people, 8 weeks, and a paste rather than whole figs
The abstract gives no sizes of effect, and doesn't say what else the paste contained or who funded it

A 2022 meta-analysis of fruit trials judged the trial at low risk of bias, but listed it among trials in which fruit did not clearly change stool form or frequency; its pooled benefit on stool form came from kiwifruit
The other trials tested fig syrups, which are cooked preparations and a different product, in small groups for 2 to 4 weeks
Colon transit time is a measurement, though it relates directly to the complaint
findings.summary: In a double-blind trial in Korea, 80 adults with functional constipation ate a fig (Ficus carica) paste or a placebo for 8 weeks. Compared with placebo, the fig paste went with a shorter colon transit time (how long food takes to pass through the large bowel), better stool type and less abdominal discomfort; blood tests and checks for organ harm stayed normal. The abstract gives no sizes of these differences. A 2022 meta-analysis of 11 fruit trials included this one, rated its risk of bias low, but described it among trials in which fruit did not clearly change stool consistency or frequency; in its pooled analysis, kiwifruit, not fig paste, improved stool form. Two small trials tested fig syrup, a different product: in 90 pregnant women with constipation, 15 mL of fig syrup or fig-walnut syrup each night for 14 days went with more bowel movements and better quality of life than placebo; in 60 children, fig syrup and red sugar worked about the same for stool frequency.
findings.bottomLine: One placebo-controlled trial in 80 adults found that a fig paste shortened the time food took through the bowel and improved stool type over 8 weeks. A meta-analysis didn't count it as clearly changing stool form or frequency, and the evidence is thin.
findings.label: Constipation
findings.line: Faster bowel transit and better stools in one trial of fig paste

whyThisGrade: One trial in one country
Single-blind: patients knew whether they were eating figs, and the outcomes were symptom questionnaires
Abdominal pain severity, a main IBS symptom, did not improve
The abstract gives no sizes of effect
findings.summary: In a single-blind randomised trial, 150 adults with irritable bowel syndrome with constipation were split into three groups for 4 months: dried figs (45 g twice a day, according to two reviews), flixweed seed, or a control group. Compared with the control group, figs went with better scores on the IBS severity scale, less frequent pain, less bloating, better bowel frequency, fewer hard stools, better quality of life and more satisfaction with bowel habits. Pain severity and CRP (an inflammation marker) did not change. Figs and flixweed did about as well as each other. A 2023 systematic review of herbal remedies for IBS-C included the trial and judged the overall evidence for such remedies to be of limited quality.
findings.bottomLine: In one Iranian trial of 150 adults with IBS with constipation, eating dried figs every day for 4 months went with fewer symptoms and better quality of life than no figs, though pain severity didn't change and patients knew what they were eating.
findings.label: Irritable bowel with constipation
findings.line: Fewer symptoms in one trial of 150 adults; pain severity didn't change

findings.population: US adults with raised LDL cholesterol (dried figs); US adults with overweight and at least one other heart risk factor (mixed dried fruit)
whyThisGrade: Two short trials (4 and 5 weeks) with 83 and 55 people
Only one tested figs alone; in the other, figs were a quarter of a dried fruit mix
The dried fruit trial was funded by dried fruit industry boards, including the California Fig Advisory Board, which contributed to its design
The fig trial was not blinded (people knew when they were eating figs)
findings.summary: In a crossover trial, 83 adults aged 30 to 75 with raised LDL cholesterol added 120 g of dried California Mission figs a day to their usual diet for 5 weeks and ate their usual diet for another 5 weeks. LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol and triglycerides did not differ between the two periods; total cholesterol tended to rise with figs, but only in people who had the usual diet first. Soluble fibre intake rose from 8.2 to 12.6 g a day, sugars from 23.4% to 32.2% of energy, and body weight did not change. In a second crossover trial, 55 adults with overweight and another heart risk factor ate three-quarters of a cup a day of mixed dried plums, figs, dates and raisins or a starchy snack with the same energy, for 4 weeks each: blood fats did not differ between the two, although LDL was 0.10 mmol/L higher than at the start during the dried fruit period.
findings.bottomLine: In a 5-week trial in 83 adults with high LDL cholesterol, adding 120 g of dried figs a day did not lower LDL or triglycerides, and total cholesterol tended to rise. A trial of mixed dried fruit including figs also found no change in blood fats.
findings.label: LDL cholesterol and triglycerides
findings.line: No fall in LDL or triglycerides in a 5-week trial

studies.title: Effect of consumption of dried California mission figs on lipid concentrations.

findings.population: US adults with overweight and another heart risk factor (mixed dried fruit); 12 healthy Greek adults (one meal containing dried figs)
whyThisGrade: No trial of figs on their own could be checked: a 2023 review, funded by the California Fig Advisory Board, describes one in type 2 diabetes that isn't indexed in Europe PMC
In the only longer trial, figs were a quarter of a dried fruit mix, so the result is for dried fruit in general
That trial was funded by dried fruit industry boards, including the California Fig Advisory Board
The meal study measured a whole dessert with currants and dried figs in 12 people, once
findings.summary: In a 4-week crossover trial of 55 adults with overweight and another heart risk factor, three-quarters of a cup a day of mixed dried plums, figs, dates and raisins went with fasting blood sugar 0.08 mmol/L higher (95% confidence interval 0.005 to 0.16 higher) than a starchy snack with the same energy and carbohydrate, a very small difference; fasting insulin, blood pressure and weight change did not differ. In a crossover study of 12 healthy adults, a traditional Greek halva with currants and dried figs had a glycaemic index of 52 (low), lower than glucose; this was a whole dessert, not figs alone. Studies that lowered blood sugar after a glucose drink used fig fruit extracts standardised to abscisic acid, or fig leaf preparations, which are different products. A 2023 review describes a 2-month trial in 50 people with type 2 diabetes in which figs lowered blood sugar by 13.5%, against 27.6% with metformin; that trial isn't indexed in Europe PMC and couldn't be checked.
findings.bottomLine: There is almost no research on figs themselves and blood sugar. In a trial of mixed dried fruit including figs, fasting blood sugar was very slightly higher than with a starchy snack. Extract and leaf studies don't show what eating figs does.
findings.label: Blood sugar
findings.line: Almost no research on figs themselves; no clear change

Mineral intake came from 24-hour diet recalls, which rely on memory
Blood levels are only one way to look at mineral status
findings.summary: In the same crossover trial (88 people with data, 120 g of dried California Mission figs a day for 5 weeks), diet recalls showed more calcium and potassium in the diet during the fig period, but mineral levels in blood samples were nearly the same as during the usual diet. Figs also replaced other foods: the authors estimated that eating figs pushed out about 4% of desserts, 5% of vegetables, 10% of dairy products and 23% of grain products that people would otherwise have eaten.
findings.bottomLine: In a 5-week trial, adding 120 g of dried figs a day raised calcium and potassium in people's diets, but mineral levels in the blood didn't change. The figs also took the place of some other foods, including dairy and grains.

visuals.caption: Share of people with a positive skin-prick test to fresh or dried fig, in two groups of allergy patients: 85 with birch pollen allergy only, and 60 sensitised only to weeping fig (Ficus benjamina), a common houseplant. A positive skin test is not the same as reacting when eating figs: among birch-allergic people who tested positive to fig, 66% reported symptoms after fresh figs, while dried figs were mostly well tolerated.

visuals.title: What a fig is
visuals.caption: Figs are an unusual fruit: a closed flower head with the flowers inside. Some fig trees ripen fruit without pollination and can be grown from planted branches, which is how archaeologists think early farmers may have grown them.

steps.label: A closed flower head
steps.text: The fig develops from a closed inflorescence (a hollow flower head), which encloses hundreds of tiny flowers that bloom inside it.

steps.label: Many small fruits
steps.text: Each flower forms a tiny fruit (the crunchy 'seeds'), so a fig is a combined fruit of several hundred small ones inside a fleshy wall.

steps.label: Seedless kinds
steps.text: Some fig trees set fruit without pollination (parthenocarpy). Charred figs about 11,400 years old from such trees were found in the Jordan Valley.

steps.label: Two crops a year
steps.text: Fig trees can give an early crop on last season's growth (the breba crop) and a main crop on new growth. Over 800 varieties are grown, with skins from green to black-violet.

whoShouldBeCareful.with: Kidney disease or a potassium limit
whoShouldBeCareful.note: The UK food table lists 970 mg of potassium per 100 g of dried figs, so 2 dried figs (about 40 g) hold about 390 mg; a fresh fig (about 55 g) holds about 110 mg. If you have been told to limit potassium, talk to your doctor or renal dietitian about dried figs.

The UK food table lists 52.9 g of sugars per 100 g of dried figs, so 2 dried figs (about 40 g) hold about 21 g of sugars; a fresh fig (about 55 g) holds about 5 g. If you are managing blood sugar, talk to your doctor or dietitian about dried figs.

whoShouldBeCareful.with: Allergy to weeping fig (Ficus benjamina), birch pollen or other fruits
whoShouldBeCareful.note: Fig allergy can come with sensitisation to the houseplant weeping fig: in one allergy clinic, 2.5% of people with airborne allergies reacted to weeping fig on skin tests, and most of them also had positive skin tests to fresh figs; seven had hives, swelling or asthma after eating figs or related fruits. Kiwi, papaya, avocado, banana and pineapple can cross-react. Most of these people were not allergic to rubber latex. People with birch pollen allergy often react to fresh figs, while dried figs are mostly tolerated. If figs make your mouth itch or cause other symptoms, talk to your doctor or an allergist.

whoShouldBeCareful.with: Picking figs or pruning fig trees in the sun
whoShouldBeCareful.note: The milky sap from fig branches, leaves and fruit skin contains furanocoumarins. When it gets on the skin and the skin is then in sunlight, it can cause phytophotodermatitis: red, itchy patches and blisters, sometimes in streaks, that can leave dark marks. Case reports describe it after picking figs and pruning fig trees in the sun. This is about handling the tree, not eating the fruit.

cautions: Figs are not a treatment for constipation, diabetes or high cholesterol. Constipation that is new, persistent or comes with bleeding, weight loss or pain is worth discussing with your doctor.

Dried figs are dense in energy and sugars: in the UK food table, 227 kcal and 52.9 g of sugars per 100 g, against 43 kcal and 9.5 g for fresh figs. In the 5-week trial of 120 g of dried figs a day, sugars rose from 23.4% to 32.2% of people's energy intake.
In the trial of fig syrup in children, fig syrup caused diarrhoea more often than red sugar.
unknowns: Almost no trials have tested eating whole figs, fresh or dried. Two trials looked at constipation (one used a paste), and two at blood fats and minerals; none measured heart disease, diabetes or other illness.

The constipation trials were small, done in Korea and Iran, and their abstracts don't give sizes of effect. Whether figs ease constipation as much as other high-fibre fruits such as prunes or kiwifruit has not been tested head to head.

Most studies behind health claims for figs used fig leaves, leaf tea, fig fruit extracts, latex or animals. Those are different from eating the fruit, and their results can't be taken as results for figs. A fig and olive oil preparation tested in rheumatoid arthritis is also a different product.
Fresh figs are barely studied apart from their chemistry: nearly all eating trials used dried figs or fig products.
The UK food table has no vitamin K value for figs, so this page can't say how much vitamin K a portion holds or whether it matters for blood thinners.

A 2023 review of fig research was funded by the California Fig Advisory Board, and the dried fruit trial was funded by dried fruit industry boards that helped design it. Who funded the Korean fig paste trial isn't stated in its abstract.

It isn't known which compounds explain any effect. The food table measures sugars, minerals and some vitamins, but none of the polyphenols, ficin or furanocoumarins, and a food has thousands of compounds no table tracks.
